title: Beyond a Decade of MENACTRIMS: Scientific Achievements, Publicly Documented Implementation Gaps, and a Roadmap to a Regional Learning Health System
content: Background: The Middle East North Africa Committee for Treatment and Research in Multiple Sclerosis (MENACTRIMS) has developed congresses, clinical guidance, registry research, training, certification, and advocacy partnerships. Evaluating this infrastructure requires distinctions between organizational activity, implementation, and attributable benefit.Objectives: To characterize documented achievements, compare the geographic distribution of major functions, identify public reporting gaps, and propose a measurable regional learning-health-system roadmap.Methods: A structured public-document audit and targeted literature synthesis covered activities from 2014 through 23 August 2026, with a documented update on 16 October 2026. Sources were classified by provenance and evidentiary purpose, without performance scoring. Geographic coverage used a fixed 19-jurisdiction Middle East and North Africa frame. Reported attendance terms and registry denominators were preserved.Results: Ten completed congresses were identified; seven with exact headline attendance had a median of 934 participants (interquartile range 761.5–1006.5). Seven congresses were hosted in the United Arab Emirates. Five major guideline outputs or revisions, multicountry registry studies, policy endorsements, and traceable grant- and fellowship-linked publications demonstrated sustained scientific activity. The public registry headline was 15,387, compared with 14,438 enumerable center records; variable displays represented 78.8%–93.9% of the headline, without establishing true field completeness. Iran, Egypt, and Kuwait contributed 75.4% of enumerable records. Council listings covered 15/19 jurisdictions, registry centers 8/19, and certified centers 2/19. Certification standards already specify three-year renewal and prefer registry participation; fellowship terms require reporting and career follow-up. Aggregated results of these processes were less readily ascertainable.Conclusions: MENACTRIMS has established substantial regional infrastructure. Differing geographic distributions identify questions about coordination and opportunity but do not establish organizational failure. A phased roadmap for 2027–2035 should build on existing systems through denominator reconciliation, publicly reported program outcomes, guideline-linked quality improvement, and meaningful patient and professional participation. Public-source limitations and the non-systematic synthesis preclude causal attribution of regional patient outcomes to MENACTRIMS.
